title: Gradient
body:
For A function
$$
f(x,y,z)
$$
The Gradient of $f$ is defined as
$$
\nabla f= \langle \frac{ \partial f }{ \partial x } ,\frac{ \partial f }{ \partial y } ,\frac{ \partial f }{ \partial z } \rangle
$$

It is what the [[Derivative]] in [[CALCULUS 1]] becomes when the input is a vector: one slope per
input direction, collected into a vector that points the way $f$ increases fastest. That is why
[[Gradient Descent]] steps along $-\nabla f$, and why it is [[Optimization]] with more variables
rather than a different subject.

## The two properties that matter

**1. It answers for every direction, not just the axes.** The rate of change of $f$ along a unit
vector $\mathbf{u}$ is the directional derivative

$$
D_{\mathbf{u}}f = \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} = \lVert \nabla f \rVert \cos\theta
$$

a [[Dot Product]] with the direction you care about. It is largest when $\theta = 0$, so **$\nabla f$
points along the steepest ascent and $\lVert\nabla f\rVert$ is how steep that is**. Only the
$n$ [[Partial Derivative|partials]] have to be computed to answer for infinitely many directions.

**2. It is perpendicular to level sets.** Moving along a level curve leaves $f$ unchanged, so
$D_{\mathbf{u}}f = 0$ there, so the gradient is orthogonal to the level curve through the point.
That fact is used twice in this course: it is why $\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g$ in
[[Lagrange Multipliers]], and it is how the normal vector to a surface $F(x,y,z) = 0$ gets
computed. Contour lines on a map and the steepest path down a hill cross at right angles for this
reason.

At a critical point $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ and the direction information is gone, which is where
[[Multivariable Optimization]] needs the second derivatives instead.

## Related

- [[Partial Derivative]]: the components
- [[Multivariable Chain Rule]]: $df/dt = \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$, the gradient form
- [[Multivariable Optimization]] and [[Lagrange Multipliers]]
- [[Divergence]] and [[Curl]]: the other two $\nabla$ operators, both acting on
  [[Vector Field|vector fields]] rather than producing one
- [[Conservative Vector Field]]: a field that happens to be some function's gradient
- [[Vector Calculus]], [[Multivariable Calculus]], [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]
